chunks: "Because every millimetre between the supply and the load is a resistor and an inductor in series with it.

The resistor gives you DC drop: one ounce copper is about half a milliohm per square, so with a 1 volts rail at 10 amps, 20 mm of 1 mm trace each way costs roughly 190 millivolts, about a fifth of the rail.
The inductor gives you transient droop: a few nanohenries of trace and a load that steps 5 amps in 100 nanoseconds makes V equals L di by dt, so 10 nanohenries gives half a volt.
The regulator's feedback senses its own output capacitor, not the load, so it regulates perfectly at the wrong place and can't fix the drop in between.
The extra inductance also slows and can destabilise the loop's response to load steps.
And a long trace is a bigger antenna: it radiates the supply's switching noise and picks up noise from elsewhere.
So I put the regulator and its output capacitors as close to the load as the heat and noise constraints allow.
If I can't, I widen the path into planes, put capacitance at the load, use remote sense, or use a point-of-load regulator fed from a higher-voltage bus."
